title: The Squirrel at Rama's Bridge
text:
In the Ramayana, Rama's army of monkeys and bears built a bridge across the sea to Lanka to rescue Sita. A story told across India adds a small figure to that great work.

The monkeys were hauling huge boulders and whole trees and throwing them into the water. Among them, a little squirrel was also at work. Again and again it rolled in the wet sand on the shore, ran onto the half-built bridge, and shook the sand off its fur into the gaps between the stones. Then it ran back for more.

Some of the monkeys found this ridiculous. One of them laughed and pushed the squirrel aside, or in some tellings flung it away, telling it to stop getting under the feet of those doing real work.

Rama saw what happened. He picked the squirrel up gently and told the monkeys that it was helping as much as it was able, and that its few grains of sand filled the cracks between their great stones. Then he stroked its back with three fingers. Ever since, the tellers say, Indian palm squirrels have carried three pale stripes down their backs, the marks of Rama's hand.
lesson: Do not measure contributions only by their size. The person filling the small gaps may be what holds the larger work together, and they deserve thanks.
people: Rama, a squirrel, the monkey army
source: Indian folk tradition and regional Ramayana retellings
caveat: The squirrel episode is not in Valmiki's Ramayana and comes from later regional and folk tradition.
